title: EF Core vs Dapper vs raw SQL
description: Compare EF Core, Dapper, and raw SQL for data access, understanding the performance and productivity trade-offs of each approach.

data.text: EF Core is not the only tool for data access in .NET. Dapper — a lightweight micro-ORM — and plain raw SQL with `DbCommand` each have their own strengths and weaknesses. Choosing the right tool for each workload is a hallmark of senior engineering: use EF Core for productivity and maintainability, but reach for Dapper or raw SQL when raw performance or precise query control matters.

EF Core is a full-featured ORM that handles change tracking, migrations, relationship management, and LINQ translation. It excels at productivity, code-first schema evolution, and complex domain models. Its overhead comes from the translation pipeline, change tracker, and the abstraction layer between your code and the database.

Dapper extends `IDbConnection` with mapping helpers. You write the SQL yourself, and Dapper materializes the results into your POCOs. There is no change tracking, no LINQ translator, and no migration system. The result is near-raw-SQL performance with a small amount of object-mapping convenience.

data.title: Same query: EF Core vs Dapper

data.text: EF Core itself supports raw SQL through `FromSqlRaw` and `ExecuteSqlRaw`. These methods let you write exact SQL while still using the DbContext for connection management. Use raw SQL when you need database-specific features like window functions, CTEs, or bulk hints that the LINQ translator cannot express.

data.title: Raw SQL with FromSqlRaw
data.code:
var topCustomers = await dbContext.Customers
    .FromSqlRaw(@"
        SELECT c.Id, c.FullName, COUNT(o.Id) AS OrderCount,
               RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(o.Id) DESC) AS Rank
        FROM Customers c
        JOIN Orders o ON o.CustomerId = c.Id
        GROUP BY c.Id, c.FullName
        HAVING COUNT(o.Id) > @MinOrders"
    , new { MinOrders = 10 })
    .ToListAsync();

items.title: EF Core
items.description: Full-featured ORM with LINQ, migrations, and change tracking.

items.title: Dapper
items.description: Micro-ORM that maps SQL results to POCOs with minimal overhead.
cons: SQL written as strings — no compile-time safety
Manual query maintenance across schema changes

items.title: Raw SQL (FromSqlRaw)
items.description: Write exact SQL executed through EF Core's DbContext.
cons: No automatic result mapping beyond entity types
Still subject to DbContext tracking overhead

items: Use EF Core for CRUD-heavy applications, complex domain models, and rapid development where productivity outweighs raw speed.
Use Dapper for high-throughput read paths, reporting endpoints, or queries where LINQ translation produces suboptimal SQL.
Use raw SQL via FromSqlRaw for database-specific features like CTEs, window functions, or query hints that EF Core LINQ cannot express.
Mix approaches in the same application: EF Core for the write model and Dapper for reporting or analytics queries.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: EF Core maximizes productivity with LINQ, tracking, and migrations.
Dapper maximizes raw performance with minimal abstraction.
Raw SQL via FromSqlRaw gives full control while keeping DbContext benefits.
There is no universal winner — combine tools based on each workload's needs.
